utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed, Mr. Ierace, that you would like to address the Chamber this morning, but before giving you the opportunity to do so, I would like to come back to an issue raised yesterday by Mr. Stamp, that is, about the 92 bis (C) statements. The Chamber has decided that these statements can be submitted to the Chamber now. The main reason for not waiting is that then we have the statement available to the Chamber and that, if necessary, the Defence could examine witnesses also in respect of the statement, and if the Appeals Chamber would decide otherwise about the admissibility, of course, this Chamber will have to draw the consequences of that. But it is mainly in order not to bother the Defence, not to obstruct the Defence in paying proper attention to these statements while other witnesses are examined. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in relation to that issue that you raised, if you wish, we could hand copies of those two statements to the Registrar now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the decision of the Chamber was that one of the statements was only partially admitted into evidence. You only applied for a partial --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that what you are going to give to the Registrar is limited to the part you asked to submit to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will give you an opportunity. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in their present form, they are the entire statement. If you wish, we could redact the statement appropriately so that it contains only the part upon which we rely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that that would be better, but let me first -- I saw that Mr. Piletta-Zanin was on his feet already twice, so give him an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is just to clarify things a little in relation to the statement, rather, in relation to 92 bis. Now, the Defence is wondering when is it that these documents should be submitted directly or indirectly to the witnesses. I do understand the intention of your Chamber to protect the Defence's rights, but how could we, if there was a reference to these statements in any way at the time of hearing of the next witness, if the Appeals Chamber has to decide in favour of that. Now, this is a technical question, but it will be propitious to examine it now because if the witness should be -- should know about these statements in relation to 92 bis and later the Chamber hypothetically should give right to the Defence, that would imply that a large part of the testimony - perhaps even all of the testimony - of the witness who knew about this report could be put into question, and so this would be a problem that would come by consequence, and this is what the Defence would like to tell your Chamber at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your problem, or at least I do understand what you think will be our problem as well. If it is not admitted at this moment, it would be more difficult for the Chamber to understand part of the testimony that might be related to the statements. If during the examination of witnesses still to be examined attention will be paid to the whole or part of these written statements by deceased witnesses, it certainly will lose part, or perhaps even all, of its relevance if finally this Chamber would have to disregard the written statements by the deceased witnesses. I do see the problem, but if we would decide otherwise and say, well, of course, we have read the statements since we had to decide on whether to admit them or not, so we have knowledge of the content of the statement, and it is up to this Chamber finally to take these statements into consideration or to disregard them, but at this very moment, the Chamber takes the view that it is better to have them on the table when these witnesses will be examined and, finally, when we know the decision of the Appeals Chamber, that we know whether we can take them into consideration and, therefore, also take into consideration those parts of future testimony which relates to that or, at least, to assess the probative value of it. We think this is a better way of dealing with it, and perhaps hearing the testimony of witnesses and not having in front of us the testimony -- the written statements to which this testimony is related. So it is a practical solution. I think part of the problem is created by the mixed system we are using in this court, where usually the admission of evidence would mean that it becomes known to what in most common law systems would be the jury, or would not become known to the jury. But since this Chamber had to decide itself on the admissibility of these written statements, so we have read them, I think it is a better solution to have them in front of us and to have them available to us while hearing the testimony of witnesses still to come and, at a later stage, we will finally have to decide on whether we have to disregard them or whether they may have any probative value and this, of course, is also true for the testimony still to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first matter I wish to raise concerns today's testimony table. Although the estimates which we have provided of the length of examination-in-chief in relation to the two next witnesses, Goran Todorovic and Witness J, should take us to the conclusion of today's sitting, I anticipate that because of our efficient approach, we may indeed, finish them earlier. The third witness, Mr. Magnusson, has arrived this morning -- was due to arrive this morning following a long international flight, and I anticipate he will not be ready to enter the witness box until tomorrow morning. Therefore, it may be that the evidence today finishes before the allocated time simply because we were able to keep the witnesses well within the estimates we have given. Mr. President, another matter I wish to raise concerns the issue of the timetable for the presentation of the Prosecution's case, that is, the balance of the case. I indicated that, by early this week, I would present to you a revised timetable and would make submissions in relation to what time, any time extension that we needed, should we need any extension. Given the order of the Trial Chamber some weeks ago and a communication that we received from the senior counsel in chambers approximately a week ago, it seems clear to us that we are required at this stage to finish the case by the 5th of July. That presents some difficulties to the Prosecution, but we are doing our best to contain the remainder of the case within that time period. As I indicated to the Trial Chamber, I think it was last week, we have identified some 40 witnesses that we are prepared to drop from the Prosecution list. Even so, the remaining number at our present rate of evidence - and I factor into that time taken by the Defence, as well as the Prosecution - means that we could not finish within the proposed conclusion date of the 5th of July. Mr. President, that situation has caused us to think creatively as to how we might manage to nevertheless remain within that closing date. I have a proposal which I will develop tomorrow morning, but I think it wise to alert the Trial Chamber to it today so that you have the opportunity to think about it in advance, if you so wish. Firstly, might I make these observations about the remaining witnesses generally because there are some characteristics which distinguish them from the majority of witnesses we have so far called. It could fairly be said that the average time that each of the remaining witnesses would take, if we were to approach their examination-in-chief in the same fashion as the witnesses we have already called, would be far in excess of the average time of witnesses so far. That is because of the nature of their evidence. We have a number of expert witnesses and the remainder, by and large, are what one might call international witnesses, that is, individuals who were present during the indictment period in and around Sarajevo, but who came from outside that territory, people such as United Nations military officers and UNPROFOR officers and United Nations civil affairs officers. So there is a difficulty that we have. I have a proposal which is that, where possible, with these witnesses when examined in chief, I or whichever counsel takes them for the Prosecution team elicits from them in leading form whether they are in a position to give evidence on certain topics, to which I anticipate the answer will be "yes," and then, rather than take the witness further into those topics, to ask no more questions on those topics, but instead take them to other material. The topics which would be skimmed over in that fashion would be topics which have not been the subject of cross-examination previously when similar evidence has been given by other witnesses. When I say it has not been the subject of cross-examination, I specifically mean Rule 90, and I rely upon the interim judgment that you have provided to the Defence, that is, that the Defence is required to contradict the witness, witness's evidence, where it is inconsistent with the Defence case. Therefore, the remaining area which the witness would be invited to expand upon would be the essence of their evidence which the Prosecution cannot do without. Some witnesses would still take considerable time in the witness box when examined in chief, perhaps an hour, two hours, perhaps three, but by the same token, a large number of witnesses may be dealt with well within an hour, perhaps within half an hour. If this is to work, then, it will be because the Defence is similarly restricted in cross-examination. There have been many occasions over the last few weeks and months when cross-examination has taken more time than examination-in-chief and, more particularly, where there have been repeated objections made in particular by the Defence, which has had the effect of impacting adversely on the Prosecution timetable. I do not suggest for a minute that it is inappropriate per se for the Defence to make objections or, on occasion, for the Defence to cross-examine longer than the time taken in chief. We accept, of course, that that is the approach taken by this Trial Chamber, that there be time limits on both parties, and we do our best to work within that. I simply make this observation at this stage: That my proposal will only work if the Defence is restricted in its cross-examination in the same way as the Prosecution is restricted in its examination-in-chief in this delicate remainder of the Prosecution case. Mr. President, more specifically in relation to the witness list, it is taking considerable time, as perhaps you might expect, as we juggle which witnesses we can drop and those that we really must call to some extent. I will have a final list, with one exception, tomorrow morning. That list will have a number of deletions from the remainder of the witness list. It will have one or two additions, for reasons which I will explain, and by the end of the week, there may be, and I stress "may be" an addition. And if that is the case -- a further addition, and if that is the case, I will explain why at the relevant time that is done, later in the week rather than tomorrow. Mr. President, I hasten to add that I understand that you were expecting me to give you that list today, and that was my intention until it became apparent yesterday afternoon that there is some further work required, and I would be very grateful if I could have the indulgence of the Bench until tomorrow morning when I present that list. I propose to do so before I call Mr. Magnusson and I have in mind, if it is convenient to the Trial Chamber, that the giving of his evidence be something of a test of this approach. He's a UN civil affairs officer who has a statement -- who has made a statement of many pages, much of which is relevant, but in taking him through his statement, I propose to adopt the approach that I have outlined, and perhaps that would be of assistance both to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber in allowing us to test how well it works or doesn't work. Because if it doesn't work, then the sooner we realise that, the better, and we can look at what other alternatives there may be. One of the possibilities, in a general sense, is to apply yet again Rule 92 bis, and I should say in passing that the steps taken by the Prosecution assume that the witnesses we have so far sought to deal with by 92 bis, in fact, are successfully tendered. One of the problems with 92 bis is -- and applying it to the remainder of the witnesses, is that many of those witnesses give evidence of conversations, either with the accused or with senior subordinates or with, in some cases, individuals who were further up the command, the chain of command and, therefore, 92 bis would not seem to be appropriate. Mr. President, I hope that assists. If there are any questions you wish to ask me, of course I am happy to respond and I would be grateful if I could have that further indulgence of 24 hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you have time until tomorrow. Did you also discuss the practical approach you proposed with the Defence? Wouldn't it be wise to see whether you could agree on a way of proceeding which would -- which would be approved as well by the Defence? If not, of course, we will have to take decisions on that, but as you know, this Chamber always prefers to have the parties on the same line, and so if there would be an opportunity to discuss it - and I am aware that you are running out of time since you have to prepare for tomorrow - but perhaps it might be helpful to discuss the matter with Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will do that. Perhaps if it is convenient to my friends, I could meet them at the next break and we could have a preliminary discussion then. There is one other matter I should alert the Trial Chamber to which is relevant to this proposed manner of proceeding, and that is the observation that all of these witnesses, almost without exception I should say, are in -- because they are international witnesses, come from the four corners of the earth. If we are to commit ourselves to this approach, then it means we will have to have sometimes two or even three witnesses on standby, ready to come into the Trial Chamber to give their evidence as soon as the others finish. If the approach founders, then it will be organisationally disastrous to have so many witnesses waiting around. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, invisible for the transcript, I saw you nodding a firm "no," but could you please explain what was behind your nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The truth, Mr. President. The truth was behind this gesture of mine, but I would like to be more precise in reminding the Prosecution that we have had this facility called the telephone for some time now and, therefore, we could have discussed this earlier, but I have never received a telephone call from anyone and I am only finding this out this morning. So this is what I would like to remind them. The situation as it stands now, the Defence cannot accept what has been proposed. Why is that? Because what we are being proposed is to reduce the rights of the Defence in an unacceptable way, in one way. That would be applicable to witnesses that are extremely important in authorizing the Prosecution to lead the interview, that is, the testimony, the witness hearing as they see fit. Now, in this Tribunal, any other Trial Chambers, I should say in this Tribunal, I think we should follow the Rules that have been applicable so far. Now, the hearing of a witness should be conducted in a certain way. A question should be asked in a certain way, and I think that you have noticed that sometimes Defence will accept certain leading questions and that the Defence is not objecting to them. Now, we are doing this, we are not objecting, in order to gain time. We are only objecting when we see that it is absolutely necessary, and often it does seem necessary. Now, if the Prosecution doesn't have enough time to continue this hearing of witnesses by this deadline, now this is not up to the Defence to take the consequences of that. The Defence is not here to make up for the faults of the Prosecution. It is up to the Prosecution to be perhaps more concise in the questioning, to have fewer objections, to cause fewer objections, or to do something to use any of the rights that they have left, and they don't have many left. Now, certain essential elements like those that come from other cases or from files that have been given to them very late or something like that. Now, I believe this is a principal position of the Defence which is saying, "no," and no to this manner of hearing Mr. Magnusson or any other witnesses. Now, we can discuss these thing with Mr. Ierace, if he wants to. We can maybe discuss some other means of accelerating this procedure. I believe that there must be some other means of accelerating the procedure. We saw yesterday some of the questions were asked and I did not object, for instance, the photograph that we looked at and I didn't object in questions in relation to photograph because that would have been a waste of time. So I think there are other ways of accelerating the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to make two observations. At that time, first of all, things are almost never as simple as they look at first sight. So if, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are telling us that it is not the Defence who should solve the problem of the Prosecution, you are certainly right. At the same time, we all know that we grant now and then more time to the Defence in cross-examining witnesses than the time taken by the Prosecution. So, therefore, the cause of the existing problem could not be put single on one of the parties. It is an interaction of what happens in this courtroom that is related to efficient use of time now and then. It is related to the content of the testimony which would ask for other solutions than keeping very strictly to the time used by the examining party. That is one observation. So the problem is not just as simple that as if the Defence is now asked to solve the problems of the Prosecution. The second observation I would like to make is that if I understood you well, you are quite willing to discuss in a creative way the solution of the existing problems with the Prosecution. I take it that you think that there are other ways of solving or, at least, other ways of working more efficiently. With great expectations, the Chamber awaits the outcome of your discussions during this stage. It was just a preliminary matter raised, not a final discussion on how to proceed, so I think we are informed now by both parties about an initial approach of how to proceed, and I would like to leave it to that for this very moment. Is there any other issue to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Might I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then since Mr. Stamp is the only one left, I take it that he will examine the next witness. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just to say, since the witness is about to come, I would just like to use this break that the French booth translated "5th of July" as "5th of June," so I would just like to make sure that it is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would take another month from the Prosecution's case and that would not be applauded by the Prosecution. We are waiting for the next witness. It will be Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic. He is on his way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration, and the text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Todorovic. You will first be examined by counsel of the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: 10th of January, 1982.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you live, in which city do you live?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: My entire life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January of 1994, in which part of Sarajevo did you live?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the municipality Novi Grad, and the settlement was called Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your address then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Klara Zetkin number 6. Today it is called Bosanska Street number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe the witness said he lived nearby something called the phase-C, and I see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Basically, the French and the English translation interpretation did not correspond. Could you please repeat the question to the witness so that we can clear up this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live at Klara Zetkin number 6, today, Bosanska Street number 6, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question, but at any rate, the street is currently called Bosanska Street number 6, and previously it was called Klara Zetkin Street number 6, so the house number remains same, but the street has changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Alipasino Polje was divided into different phases. Which phase is that address at?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Phase-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the 22nd of January 1994?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to describe for the Court what, if anything, happened to you that day. Did you leave your home that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I am not quite sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You lived in an apartment at Klara Zetkin number 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom did you live?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I lived with my father, mother and older brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you leave your apartment to go anywhere that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I went out to the playground or, rather, to the parking that was in front or nearby my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you play there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alone or with other persons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There were many other children there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of the children that were playing with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it has been a long time since then. I don't think I can remember the names of all of the children. But I remember that there was Mirza there who died; Nermin, who also died as a result of that incident, and there was a boy called Dzenad, there as well, Alen. I can't remember the names of all of the children who were there, but there was a total of perhaps 10 of us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any girls there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of any of the girls that were there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There was Lejla there and there were two other girls, but I truly cannot remember their names now. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you playing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We were mostly throwing snowballs at each other and sledding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were there, did you hear anything or did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard explosions of a shell. Since the sound of the shell resonated between the buildings, we were unable to assess where the explosion came from but, however, we could tell that it was quite near.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear one explosion or more than one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Actually, later on, I learned that there were two explosions. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the time being, please tell us what you heard at that time. While you were playing there with your friends, did you hear one explosion or more than one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: One explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said later on you learned something. What did you learn later on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We actually heard that those were two shells that exploded, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this question should not be allowed. This is hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no general rule against hearsay, so could you please indicate why this hearsay evidence is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that the witness is talking about an important fact, an important incident that he has personal experience of, and what happened afterwards does not concern this Chamber. This Chamber should be concerned by the personal experience of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is there anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no response to it, really. The question has been answered and I would submit that whatever weight the Court deems fit to give to that statement, the Court will do so in its best judgment. This is not the first time I have heard hearsay in this Court and I am not aware of any general rule against its admissibility, really. It is a matter of the way it is interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, if you allow me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is really urgent, but I would rather that you not interfere with whatever discussions. But if it relates to what you heard at that time, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me explain. When I said that I heard one and perhaps more of those shells fall, this is how it goes. When the shell falls between the buildings, you can hear it resonate, you can hear a sound of this nature. So it is hard to say how many shells have, in fact, fallen because it resonates quite a lot and it resonates between the buildings, so it is hard to say right away whether it is one shell or more. You can simply make an assumption, and that is all. And these shells fell immediately, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you heard this shell or shells explode, did yourself and your friends do anything?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We started running towards a safe place, which was the entrance of our apartment building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you ran towards your apartment building, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I managed to reach the building as the second shell fell. I was wounded at that time and this is what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the building did you manage to reach when the shell fell?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I almost made it into the building. It happened right at the entrance into the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were your friends that you were playing with?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were mostly behind me. They didn't make it. They didn't manage to enter the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the shell exploded behind you, did you feel or hear anything?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I felt stress. However, I didn't feel right away that I had been wounded. The explosion shook me because it was quite nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I simply ran through the entrance and I tried to get to my house up the staircase as soon as possible because I supposed that my parents would be worried about me. This was simply my instinctive thinking. I simply ran through the entrance and started running up the staircase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you meet anyone on the staircase?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I reached the 6th floor or so, I realised that I had been wounded, that there was blood running down my face. I wiped it and I saw blood on my fingers and I started feeling faint, and at that moment my father started coming down the staircase, so he was the first person that I saw on the staircase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father take you anywhere?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My father took me immediately to a nurse who lived on the 8th floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did she do anything in respect to your injury?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: She said it was not wise to touch the wound at that moment because it needed surgery. So she said she would just try to stop the bleeding, and she put a kind of a bandage, a gauze, to my wound and said professionally qualified people needed to attend to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you remain in the nurse's apartment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you remain there for half an hour, do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Because we were afraid that another shell could explode.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that half hour elapsed, did your father take you anywhere?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He took me to the military medical institution where they attended to my wound and sutured it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this institution? What is it called and where is it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was the former barracks Viktor Bubanj, and it was perhaps one, one and-a-half kilometres from my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you treated at this medical facility?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we hear again the name of the barracks because one of the booths failed to interpret that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slowly repeat the names of the barracks, Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was called Viktor Burban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there, were you discharged and sent home or were you admitted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to a room there. So this cleaning and surgery of my wound took perhaps some 15 minutes, and I was discharged immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the doctors take anything from your wound?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell at that time. There was a shrapnel there and they had to clean it and remove bits and pieces and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return there for treatment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think it was 10 or 15 days later when I went to have the -- when I went to have them check my wound and remove the stitches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your father was taking you out of the building, did you notice any at the front of the building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know what you have in mind. Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did notice. What did you notice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you mean the building in which I lived and not the medical institution where I went to have my wound attended to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When your father was taking you away from Klara Zetkin Street number 6, did you notice anything in front of the building that you lived at?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Since this was all done in haste, I managed to take a quick look at the place where the shell landed and I saw traces of blood, I saw sled there; I think there was a children's shoe there, a tennis shoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your friends that were playing with you, who were behind you as you entered your building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that some of them died, but I didn't know at the time exactly who had died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember the names of those who died?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The names of the children who were my friends: There was Mirza there, and then another boy called Mirza as well, a boy called Nermin. There were two girls whom I didn't know personally, however, I used to see them in front of my building, and they were somewhat younger than me so I didn't know them fully well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know their names, the two girls?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know at that time but I learned their names later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Their names were Indira -- and I can't remember the name of the other girl right now. I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were you the only -- was your group of children the only group of children that was outside playing that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was the only one, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day in the parking area in front of your building, did you see any soldiers or any military activity taking place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of last year, did you participate in the production of a video on which you indicated to an investigator of the OTP certain places which are relevant to this incident that you just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with your leave, may I proceed to show the witness and have him identify Exhibit P3281.G?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, leave is granted, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems as if the -- if it is important, the number is P3281.G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have in words now on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Can you please indicate by pointing where, to the best of your recollection, you and your friends were playing on the 22nd of January, 1994. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Can you please indicate by pointing where, in which direction, to the best of your recollection, you and your friends started running after you heard the first shell explode on the 22nd of January, 1994. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Thank you. Can you now please show me by standing at the location where, to the best of your recollection, the shell which wounded you exploded on the 22nd of January, 1994. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Mr. Todorovic, can you now please show me by walking to and standing on the spot where, to the best of your recollection, you were located when you were wounded on the 22nd of January, 1994. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Can you walk to the spot and stand there. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: I am now going to mark that spot with yellow paint in the figure of an X with a 1 beside it."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. President, with your leave, I propose also to show the witness a photograph and ask if he can identify that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I do so, may I just for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The places that you indicated in the video that you just saw, I take it you did so to your best recollection and knowledge. Is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could photograph P3678.D be shown? Slowly turn it clockwise. And slowly turn it clockwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If and when you see the spot where you were injured, please tell us to stop.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the spot where you were injured at?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? How do you mean, to describe it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us where it was. Do you see the spot on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the spot on the photograph. I don't know how to describe it. I could perhaps indicate that it is on the right-hand side of the screen. It is the entrance, the only entrance on that part of the screen that can be seen from this angle. This is the spot where I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the area where there is a motor car parked?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, behind the car, in front of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you continue turning. Could you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area where the cars are parked, is that the park in front of the building that you were playing at?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the parking lot. Yes, except it was the upper part of the parking lot. The photograph should be turned to the left-hand side to show the exact area where we played.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please turn it slightly to the left.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is it, if you can describe the place on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The spot is located exactly underneath or beneath the chimney, which can be seen quite well, so it is on the parking lot, but it is in the direction of the chimney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you continue to turn to the right. Could you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The street which runs towards a building in the background of the photograph, is that Cetinska Street?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It is not the entire street. Cetinska goes approximately -- in fact, it begins from there, from the second lamp post. So from that post that we can see going from here. So Klara Zetkin Street goes towards this side, like that. Towards me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it from your answer that this is a true and accurate photograph of the area in front of your apartment building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further in chief, may it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp. Ms. Pilipovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you will now be examined by counsel for the defence. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer this question: On the 22nd of January, 1994, how many of the children were playing in this area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot quite remember. I cannot recall. I didn't count the people. I didn't think it was necessary. But there were about 10 of us or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, you told us -- answered by my learned colleague that you heard one explosion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that in the statement that you gave to the investigators of the OTP on the 18th of September, 2001, that in that statement you said that you heard two explosions, could you perhaps answer what is true? What is the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I said that I heard two explosions, of course, what happened is that I learned two explosions happened. I heard about it later after the incident. I heard there were two shells later. Because they were resonating, there was -- the sound was deflected so it was impossible to tell how many shells had fallen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that you learned about it later that two shells had landed and that it was on the basis of that that you told the investigators that two explosions had taken place, could you perhaps tell us, did you hear where these shells had fallen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was not possible to tell where they had fallen. You mean did I tell them? I am not sure that I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question: When I told you that you told the investigators of the OTP that you heard that there were two explosions and today, at the question of my learned colleague, you said that you had heard only one explosion. Now, considering this difference, you told us that it was later that you heard that two shells had landed and it was on the basis of that that you said that there were two explosions. Now, if I have not interpreted you correctly, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It is okay. Now, when the Prosecutor asked the questions, this was not -- this kind of question, it wasn't when I heard it or how many I heard, how many explosions I heard. The question wasn't what I knew then and what I knew now. That was not -- that was not stressed as being very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you answered that you learned later since you heard that there were two explosions -- two shells, as you said, could you perhaps tell us where did they fall, these two shells, that you learned about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They landed behind the building where I lived. So we played in front of the building where I lived and they fell behind the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "on the other side on the other building, behind the building," could you perhaps clarify for us what is located behind your building, on the other side of the building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: What is located is a small kind of park.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where this kind of park is, could you tell us whether that area, that park, has a name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps later, as you say, that you learned that two shells had landed there, did you learn whether anyone was injured by the landing of these two shells?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "no," does that mean that you didn't learn anything or that nobody was injured?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't learn, I didn't find out, nor did I enquire about anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area where you played and where you were sledding, we saw that area on the video material and on the circular photograph. Now, in that area, do you know in that area where the shell landed and how many shells landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean throughout the war or -- ?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 22nd of January.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They came -- they fell in that area, those two shells, and then two also fell in another street, lower down. But that is quite some way away from where the two shells landed that had to do with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I showed you the circular photograph again, could you perhaps indicate on the circular photograph in relation to the place where you were injured, could you perhaps tell us where these two shells landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in the area where I was wounded?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The first shell that landed cannot be seen in that area. You cannot see the spot of the explosion of the second shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say it cannot be seen, the spot where the second shell landed, could you see perhaps where the first shell landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the camera was actually located on the spot where the first shell landed. Where the photograph was taken from, the camera was located on this spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to show the witness Prosecution evidence 9281, that is the 360-degrees photograph. We can be shown the spot of the first --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what -- I made a mistake. I made a mistake with the spots. Where the first to where the second landed, I think I made a mistake with the two of them. So perhaps if we can show on the photograph, I think I may have mistaken first for the second. You can see -- so this is the second shell that I am talking about. The first one landed behind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Slow down a moment. You have at a very high speed. Mr. Todorovic, everything you say has to be translated first. So if you immediately answer the question, then the interpreters have no time to translate the question, and the same is true for Ms. Pilipovic. So would you please take a pause now and then. Ms. Pilipovic, did you want to show the witness again the 360-degree photograph we just saw?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The circular photograph, yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is on my screen under computer evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is P3678.D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is "D", not "G"? On my list, it is "G." Did you want to show the video or the circular photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Circular photograph, Your Honour. But what I have put on is that the video was 3281.G.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you have a photograph before you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, now that you can see the photograph before you, this hill at the background of the photograph behind these two high-rise buildings, could you tell us what is the name of the hill?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I think that is Zuc hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, here in this part of the photograph, could you indicate for us the spot where, according to you, the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Which shell?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You cannot see it in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the second?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The second fell on the spot where the camera is located now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask for the photograph to go to the right, please. If the cursor could be moved to the right, please. Mr. Todorovic, you tell us as we going around with the photograph when to stop.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You can stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that it is in this part, according to you, the second shell landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It fell behind the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Behind the building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, on this photograph, can you indicate on this photograph where the shell landed from which you had injuries and your friends had injuries?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is located on the spot, the spot where the video is -- where the camera, where the cameraman is located.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask to continue the circular movement of the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you tell us when to stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, could we stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, could you tell us, this hill that we can see in the background behind these houses, could you tell us what is the name of the hill?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you continue, please, the circular movement of the photograph to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you tell us when. Can you see it at the time that this is going around? Can you see the spot where the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Which shell?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The shell you suffered injuries from.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You cannot see it because the spot is where the cameraman is standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, he has now five times said that the actual spot where the camera is, is the spot where the shell landed. I don't know what's the use of asking him again the same question. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am now finished with the circular photograph questioning because now I understand now that the spot that the shell landed from which the witness suffered injuries is where the cameraman is standing, and I just wanted to conclude that we cannot see this spot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us where in relation to the place that you were wounded at, how far is where the cameraman is standing, that is, how far is the spot from where the shell landed to the spot where you were injured, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: 10 to 15 metres. That is an approximation. I never calculated it exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether on that spot -- can you see that spot? Can you see the spot? Can you see the marks from the grenade, from the shell?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure that understand. What spot and what traces?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the spot where the shell landed, is there a trace? Is there a trace from the shell?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can see the spot?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Todorovic, asked by my learned colleague, you answered that on that day when you were playing with your friends, that you did not notice soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer, please, in the period 1992, 1993 and 1994, in that area where you lived, did you see soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers were not permanently there in the building. Of course I saw soldiers passing by, not a number of them, not in convoys, but simply people from the houses went to the front line. That is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can see it is time for a break. I will have another 10 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, we will have a break for half on hour so we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed with the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, just before the break, you told us that -- before the break, you told us that you used to see soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a real full uniform. Some of them wore camouflage uniforms and tennis shoes and then an ordinary jacket on top of it, or they would only have camouflage trousers on them. It wasn't a real full uniform on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were 12 years old at the time, did you know that in the vicinity of the place where you lived, there was a military staff, a military headquarters where the troops converged?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There was definitely nothing of the sort in the vicinity of the building where I lived, but liberally speaking, I think that within a kilometre, kilometre and-a-half, there was a first front line, so there might have been some kind of headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the place where you lived, was there a restaurant called "Stela"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the area of Phase-C where you lived, there was a headquarters of a detachment known as Kulin Ban?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this part where you indicated the shell had landed, can you tell me how far was it from that spot and to the premises where the headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, perhaps some 500 metres. Perhaps more than that. I don't know. I can't tell you exactly. I don't know. I can't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today that the shell that inflicted injuries on you and your friends was the second one that landed. Have you learned later on where the first shell had landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Or, rather, not the exact spot. I was simply told that it landed behind the building, but I don't know the exact spot where it landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you told us that in relation to the place where you were injured, the second grenade, the second shell, landed some 10 metres away, so can you tell me in relation to the first grenade, how far is it from there, where the second shell landed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I was told that it landed behind the building, but I never saw the exact spot because, for a month after my being wounded, I didn't go out of the building. And the second shell landed on the grassy area so that the traces of its landing were gone soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that in relation to the place where you lived, the front line was about 1 kilometre away?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately 1 kilometre, perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you tell us that, is this your personal knowledge or is this something that you learned from somebody from your family or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I learned that later. During the war, we knew approximately where the front line was, and after the war, I went to the place where the front line was and I saw where it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you told us that the first grenade landed on a spot that is hard to identify right now because there is no trace left, can you tell us this: This spot where the first shell landed, can you tell us how far is it from the headquarters of the Kulin Ban detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mean with respect to the first shell?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly because I don't know the exact spot where the first shell landed. I simply know that it landed behind the building, but I don't know exactly where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the incident which took place on the 22nd of January, 1994, can you tell us whether around that time or immediately thereafter anybody spoke to you about the incident which took place? Did you talk to anybody about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was it that you spoke to somebody and gave information regarding this incident for the first time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly, but it could have been a year after the incident that I gave my first statement. I can't tell you exactly. It is hard to pinpoint it. I know that it was definitely a year or more than a year, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question: When you told us that you heard the explosion, you couldn't tell whether it was one or two explosions, but can you tell us whether you heard where the shell was fired from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "I can't remember," does this mean that you did not hear where it was fired from or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this statement you gave to the OTP investigators on the 18th of September, 2001, you said, "I didn't hear the firing of the shell." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether that is true, the fact that you said that you didn't hear where it was -- where it had been fired from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any member of your family a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you quoted the witness for the first time, it reads in English that he would have said, "I didn't hear the firing of the shell." In your second question, it reads in English: "Can you tell us whether that is true, the fact that you said that you didn't hear where it was where it had been fired?" The first quotation is about whether he heard the shell being fired. The second quotation is about a direction. Could you please inform the Chamber whether the first or the second one is correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my first question was a full quotation of the witness's words in the statement given to the investigators on the 18th of September, 2001, and this is paragraph 4 of the document of his statement, where in paragraph 2, the witness is recorded as saying, "I did not hear the shells being fired." And I wanted the witness to confirm whether this was true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in your second question, your quote was a bit different, and there is some relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is my interpretation. The first time I quoted and the second time I interpreted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you told us that some members of your family were members of BH army or that your father was a member of it; did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether your father had a uniform?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Not a full uniform, but he had some parts of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was issued weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. Or rather, the weapons were not normally brought home and he typically did not go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how much time during a day or during a week your father spent in his unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I think that it was every other day that he went there. But I don't know exactly. I can't remember. But at any rate, he spent quite a bit of time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he went to serve there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I meant is that he would go there every other day, so he would be at home a day and at the front line for the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say that he went to the front line, can you tell us where your father slept at night?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly. I never accompanied him, so I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father tell you where the front lines were, the ones where he was at?

utterances.speaker: GORAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that fully, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Todorovic, since the Chamber has no further questions to you, this concludes your testimony as a witness in this court. You have answered the questions of both parties and, well, you will be certainly aware that it is important for us to hear from those who were present at the relevant times, at the relevant places, to hear from those persons the answers to the questions of both parties. I thank you very much for coming to The Hague. I know it is quite a distance, it is quite a journey, and I hope you have a safe journey home again. Mr. Usher, could you please lead Mr. Todorovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, as far as I can see, we have two, I couldn't say documents, but two objects to be admitted. Could you please guide us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3678.D, 360 degree Quicktime movie; Exhibit P3281.G, video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Now, regarding the 360-degrees photograph, apart from the usual objection that we have, we believe that you also noticed that this photograph seemed to have been made - and it comes across from the testimony from this witness - not in the usual way but in some other way. And now to demonstrate this, now, I would like to point out that very often we can see the shadow which -- from where the photograph was taken and then we can see from where the trace that couldn't be seen. And now this witness said that the person who was the cameraman, that he was on the spot taking the photograph. Now, I believe that I can remember that Mr. Lesic, the expert who came to testify, told us that there was a system with a tripod and that there was a special angle so that this photograph can be taken and that then photographs are taken in a series and they are pieced together. Now, this photograph shows us that this was not taken in the usual way because we can see the shadow of the person taking the picture. We do not see the tripod at the certain number of degrees, the way that it was explained to us before. And I just wanted to make sure that the Trial Chamber also noticed this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do you want to make any observation in relation to this specific objection against the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I have no observations to make except that I would submit that it is adequate that the witness can testify where it was taken from and that it is a fair and accurate depiction of the area in front of his home where the incident happened. If it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to pay full attention to your remark, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you explain to us what makes you believe that the photographer would have the camera in his hands, instead of standing next to the tripod?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this comes out from the testimony of the witness who just testified, of Mr. Todorovic, and I believe that we can see very well on the photograph itself the shadow of a person holding with his two hands, at the height of the face, that is, fixing a camera, or at least what seems to be a camera. So we can see this shadow on the surface on the image of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that we saw a shadow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps just look at it again so that we have a better picture of the one who is supposed to take the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could look for it in the transcript. I believe that in the English transcript it is possible to see where there is somebody said that -- or the witness said that there was a person standing, and if it is necessary, I can look it up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that there is hardly any -- well, let's just first look at the 360-degrees photograph and perhaps where it is facing the building, because that is approximately where I remember that -- Could you please turn it to the right, up until we are facing the building because there it is where I remembered I saw some shadows. No. Could you please also turn a bit downwards because I noticed that sometimes you can go a bit higher up. Perhaps go a bit downwards and then back to the left. To move to the -- no, no, no. It is not zooming in, but going more to the ground level, so as low as possible. That is the lowest? There we are. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a lot clearer earlier, Mr. President. We were able to see better before. But I believe that we can see the right hand of the photograph and the left hand of the cameraman. I think that here we can see the gesture of someone who is holding their hand in front of their face with what looks to be a camera. And the testimony of Mr. Todorovic a moment ago was precisely this: [In English] "where the cameraman is standing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cameraman is not the same as someone holding a camera, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did hear the testimony of the witness but your interpretation is not a reflection of just the words, but is an interpretation. Is this the most lower? As we can't go any further down? Could you zoom in -- out? Is there any zooming out? No. It doesn't give us any extra information. Well, at least we have seen it. We have heard the interpretation of the Defence of this shadow. Is there any need for you, Mr. Stamp, to comment on the shadow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no further comments to make, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no further comments to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having listened carefully to the additional objection of the Defence and having looked again to the picture, the Chamber has decided that the 360-degree photograph will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will just give a short reason for the decision as well, and that is that it has -- the Chamber is not able to interpret the shadow we have just seen as a circumstance that would indicate that this 360-degrees photograph is not taken according to the explanation given to us before on the production of these 360-degrees photographs. That means that both the video and the 360-degree photograph just mentioned by the Registrar are admitted into evidence. Mr. Stamp, that means we are now at a point where you could call your next witness, which would be protected witness "J."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, for whom the Chamber has granted the use of a pseudonym and facial distortion during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there is no voice distortion, I think we can just proceed. Is the face distortion effective at this moment? It is. So then would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would just like to make use of this short break to say that in French transcript, in line 25, page 36, things were added which were not included and I would like to just make sure that the booth is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am certain that the proper care will be taken to listen with even more precision during the work on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. J, as I will call you because, in this courtroom, we will not use your own name, as a result of protective measures granted in respect of you. I also inform you that on the video screen that is broadcasted, your face will not be visible. Mr. J, I should have started to ask you whether you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, Mr. J, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, and the text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr. J, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher show the witness the document marked P3684, which contains the witness identifying information for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness J, I just asked -- I know you just said "yes." If you could verify that your name and date of birth are as listed on that sheet, without saying that information out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name and surname and my date of birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness J. Could you tell us in what city you were living at the time the war broke out in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
